title: Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh
summary: Dying Jacob adopts Joseph’s two sons as his own, crosses his hands to set the younger before the elder, and promises Joseph that God will bring Israel home.
historicalContext: Jacob is now about 147 years old and in his seventeenth year in Egypt (47:28). Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph and Asenath before the famine began (41:50-52), so they are young men of roughly twenty, raised at the Egyptian court yet still unattached to the covenant family by any formal act. Adoption within a family was a recognized custom in the ancient Near East; legal texts from the region record a grandfather taking a grandson as his own heir, and placing a child on or beside the knees served as a public sign that the child now belonged to the one who received him. A patriarch’s final blessing carried legal and spiritual weight, deciding inheritance and leadership. The firstborn’s double share had been forfeited by Reuben (35:22; 1 Chronicles 5:1-2), and Jacob’s act here transfers it to Joseph through his two sons, who will later count as two full tribes when Canaan is divided.
literaryContext: Genesis 48 belongs to the deathbed scenes that close the book: Jacob’s burial oath (47:29-31), the blessing of Joseph’s sons (ch. 48), the oracles over the twelve (ch. 49), and the deaths of Jacob and Joseph (ch. 50). The chapter falls into three movements, each opened by Jacob speaking to Joseph (vv. 3, 11, 21): adoption grounded in God’s promise at Bethel (vv. 3-7), the blessing with crossed hands (vv. 8-20), and a parting word of hope and inheritance (vv. 21-22). The scene deliberately recalls Genesis 27. Again an old father with failing eyes asks who stands before him, kisses the young men, and blesses the younger above the elder; yet this time the patriarch sees clearly what he is doing, and no one is deceived. The book’s long pattern of the younger preferred, from Abel and Isaac to Jacob and Perez, reaches its last instance here.
themes: The blessing passed on by faith
The Shepherd and Redeemer of Jacob’s life
Hope that outlives the patriarch’s death
The promised land as Israel’s true home

outline.title: Joseph Comes to His Dying Father
outline.summary: Told that Jacob is ill, Joseph brings Manasseh and Ephraim, and Israel gathers his strength and sits up on the bed.

outline.title: Two Grandsons Become Sons
outline.summary: Recalling God Almighty’s promise at Luz, Jacob claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own heirs, equal to Reuben and Simeon, and remembers Rachel’s death near Bethlehem.

outline.title: The Lads Received and Embraced
outline.summary: Jacob asks who the young men are, receives them as God’s gift, kisses and embraces them, and Joseph bows before his father.

outline.title: Crossed Hands and the Greater Blessing
outline.summary: Jacob deliberately lays his right hand on the younger Ephraim, invokes the Shepherd God and the redeeming Angel, refuses Joseph’s correction, and sets Ephraim before Manasseh.

outline.title: A Promise of Return
outline.summary: Jacob announces his death, assures Joseph that God will be with them and bring them back to Canaan, and gives him an extra portion of land.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass after these things, that one told Joseph, Behold, thy father is sick: and he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“After these things” ties the visit to the oath at the end of chapter 47, where Jacob made Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan. How long afterward is not said, but the news that comes now is different: “thy father is sick.” Joseph lives at court, apart from Goshen, and the message reaches him through a messenger. The Hebrew word for sickness appears here for the first time in Scripture, and it falls on a man who has already outlived his wife Rachel and been told by God that Joseph would close his eyes (46:4).

Joseph’s response is immediate and purposeful. He goes, and he takes “his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.” They are no longer boys. Born before the seven years of famine (41:50), they are now about twenty, raised among the privileges of an Egyptian household, sons of a priest’s daughter. Joseph might have treated his father’s illness as a private matter between the two of them. Instead he brings the next generation to the bedside, evidently hoping that the patriarch who carries God’s promise will bless them before he dies.

The order of the names reflects Joseph’s own assumption: Manasseh, the firstborn, comes first. That order will be reversed before the chapter ends. Joseph had once named the boys to mark that God had made him forget his toil and made him fruitful in the land of his affliction (41:51-52). By bringing them to Jacob he shows that he has not forgotten his father’s house, and that he wants his sons counted among Israel, whatever their standing in Egypt.

wordNotes.explanation: A participle of chalah, “to be weak, ill.” It describes a weakening that may or may not end in death; here the context of the burial oath shows that Jacob’s illness is his last. The same word is later used of Hezekiah, who was “sick unto death” before God added years to his life, and of Elisha’s final sickness. Scripture treats illness frankly as part of life in a fallen world, without shame and without hiding the approach of death.

verses.bibleText: And one told Jacob, and said, Behold, thy son Joseph cometh unto thee: and Israel strengthened himself, and sat upon the bed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The message now travels the other way: Jacob is told, “thy son Joseph cometh unto thee.” The two reports mirror each other, and each man prepares to meet the other. Joseph sets out with his sons; the old father rouses himself from his bed.

The verse begins with “Jacob” and ends with “Israel.” The narrator does not switch names carelessly. The frail man who hears the news is Jacob, worn down by 147 years; the man who “strengthened himself, and sat upon the bed” is Israel, the name God gave him at Peniel and confirmed at Bethel (32:28; 35:10). What follows is a covenant act, the passing on of God’s promise, and he will perform it as the bearer of that name. The same shift occurred when Jacob revived at the news that Joseph lived (45:27-28).

He gathers his remaining strength for the sake of the blessing. Earlier he had bowed himself “upon the bed’s head” after Joseph’s oath (47:31); now he sits up on that same bed. A dying man who could lie still and wait chooses instead to spend what vigour he has left on his descendants’ future with God. Hebrews will remember the scene as an act of faith performed while “a dying” (Hebrews 11:21).

wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form of chazaq, “to be strong, firm.” It describes a deliberate effort to summon strength, often for a task or in a crisis. When David’s own men spoke of stoning him at Ziklag, he “encouraged himself in the LORD his God,” using the same form. Jacob’s exertion is physical, but it serves a spiritual purpose: he braces himself to bless.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said unto Joseph, God Almighty appeared unto me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before Jacob says a word about Joseph’s sons, he speaks about God. “God Almighty appeared unto me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me.” Luz is the old name of Bethel, the place where Jacob met God twice: first as a fugitive on his way to Haran, when he saw the ladder (28:10-22), and again on his return, when God renewed his new name and repeated the covenant promises (35:6-15). The title El Shaddai, the words “appeared” and “blessed,” and the promise that follows all match the second visit, recorded in chapter 35.

The point of the reminder is authority. Jacob is about to do something unusual: adopt two grandsons and set them among the tribal heads of Israel. He has no right to rearrange the inheritance of the promise on his own initiative. He does it because God blessed him and spoke to him about his seed and the land. What he passes on is God’s word, received at a particular place and time.

The phrase “in the land of Canaan” is not idle geography in an Egyptian bedroom. Jacob is lying in Goshen, surrounded by the comforts his son provided, yet his mind goes back to the land where God appeared. The whole chapter keeps turning the family’s eyes away from Egypt toward Canaan, and this verse begins that movement. The God who met Jacob there is the foundation of everything he is about to say.

wordNotes.explanation: The divine name under which God made covenant with Abraham (17:1), by which Isaac blessed Jacob as he left for Haran (28:3), and by which God renewed the promise at Bethel (35:11). The exact derivation of Shadday is uncertain, and it is wiser not to build on a single proposed root. In use, the name is tied to God’s power to give life and increase where human means fail. Exodus says the patriarchs knew God especially by this name.

verses.bibleText: And said unto me, Behold, I will make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, and I will make of thee a multitude of people; and will give this land to thy seed after thee for an everlasting possession.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob repeats what God told him: “I will make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, and I will make of thee a multitude of people; and will give this land to thy seed after thee for an everlasting possession.” Two promises stand side by side, descendants and land, the same pair that runs through every covenant word to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The language of fruitfulness and multiplying reaches back further still, to the blessing on humanity at creation (1:28), as if the original purpose of God for the human race is being carried forward through this family.

“A multitude of people” renders a phrase that speaks of an assembly or congregation of peoples. Jacob’s seed will be more than a large clan; it will become a gathered community. The word later describes Israel assembled before God in the wilderness. By the time of the exodus the first half of the promise is visibly coming true: “the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly” (Exodus 1:7).

The second half sounds strange in Egypt. The family has been given a possession in Goshen (47:11, 27), and many Egyptians have just sold their land to Pharaoh. Against both, Jacob sets an “everlasting possession” in Canaan, the land God promised to Abraham in the same words (17:8). He owns no more of it than a burial cave and a field near Shechem. His hope rests entirely on God’s word.

There is also a hint of what is coming. Jacob speaks of being made “fruitful,” and one of the young men before him bears the name Ephraim, a name built on that idea (41:52). The promise he is quoting will shortly be spoken over that very grandson. Hebrews observes that the patriarchs died “not having received the promises,” but having seen them afar off and embraced them (Hebrews 11:13).

wordNotes.term: קְהַל עַמִּים (qehal ‘ammim) — a multitude of people
wordNotes.explanation: Qahal means an assembly or congregation, a people gathered together. Isaac had prayed that Jacob would become “a multitude [qahal] of people” (28:3), and God confirmed it at Bethel with a related phrase (35:11). The same noun later names the congregation of Israel gathered at Sinai and in worship. The Greek Old Testament often renders it with ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church.

’Achuzzah is property held by right, land that is seized or grasped as one’s own. The word described Abraham’s burial plot at Machpelah (23:4, 20) and the holding Joseph secured for his family in Egypt (47:11). Joined to ‘olam, “lasting, perpetual,” it marks Canaan as Israel’s permanent inheritance, given by God’s promise to Abraham.

verses.bibleText: And now thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, which were born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt, are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And now” moves from God’s past promise to Jacob’s present act. Because God promised to make him fruitful and to give the land to his seed, Jacob claims Joseph’s sons as his own: “thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh... are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine.” The repetition “are mine... shall be mine” has the ring of a legal declaration. Two grandsons are raised to the rank of sons, each to stand as the head of a tribe with a full share in the promised land.

The careful wording matters. They are the sons “born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt.” These are the boys born during the years when Jacob thought Joseph was dead, the years he lost. They were born to an Egyptian mother, the daughter of the priest of On (41:50), and they might easily have been absorbed into Egyptian nobility. Jacob takes them out of that future and writes them into Israel. They become heirs of Abraham by an act of adoption, not by any merit of their own.

The comparison with “Reuben and Simeon” is pointed. These were Leah’s first two sons and Jacob’s eldest. Reuben had defiled his father’s bed (35:22), and Simeon had joined Levi in the slaughter at Shechem (34:25). Later Scripture explains what is happening here: Reuben’s birthright “was given unto the sons of Joseph the son of Israel,” while leadership passed to Judah (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). The double portion that belonged to the firstborn goes to Joseph, Rachel’s firstborn, by way of his two sons.

The naming of Ephraim before Manasseh is the first hint of what Jacob intends. When the tribes later receive their lands, Ephraim and Manasseh each receive an allotment, and Joseph’s house is counted twice (Joshua 14:4; 16:4). Paul uses the language of adoption for what God does for believers: those who were strangers to the promise are brought into the family and made heirs (Galatians 4:5-7).

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to me [are] they,” a short possessive declaration placed first for emphasis and then repeated (“they shall be mine”). Similar formulas of ownership appear when God claims the firstborn of Israel (“they shall be mine,” Numbers 3:13) and when he claims his people as his treasure (Malachi 3:17). Here it functions as a formula of adoption, giving the grandsons the legal standing of sons.

verses.bibleText: And thy issue, which thou begettest after them, shall be thine, and shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob draws a clear boundary around the adoption. Any children Joseph has after these two “shall be thine,” counted as Joseph’s own and not raised to the rank of tribal heads. They will “be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance,” receiving land within the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.

This is the only mention in Scripture of further children of Joseph, and nothing more is known of them. The provision shows the legal precision of the whole scene. Jacob is not opening the door for every grandson to claim tribal status; he is assigning the firstborn’s double share to Joseph in a defined form. The tribes of Israel still number twelve in their land allotments, because Levi receives cities instead of a territory (Joshua 14:3-4).

The arrangement also keeps the inheritance in the land at the centre. “Their inheritance” refers to a share in Canaan, not in Egypt. Jacob distributes territory he does not hold and that his family will not occupy for centuries. He speaks as a man who expects God to do what he said.

wordNotes.term: עַל שֵׁם אֲחֵיהֶם יִקָּרְאוּ (‘al shem ’acheihem yiqqare’u) — called after the name of their brethren
wordNotes.explanation: To be “called by” or “after” a name means to be registered under it and to share its standing and inheritance. The same idea underlies the law of levirate marriage, where a child carries on the name of a dead brother so that his name is not “put out of Israel.” Joseph’s later sons would be enrolled under Ephraim or Manasseh and hold land within those tribal portions.

verses.bibleText: And as for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died by me in the land of Canaan in the way, when yet there was but a little way to come unto Ephrath: and I buried her there in the way of Ephrath; the same is Beth-lehem.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Suddenly Jacob speaks of Rachel. “And as for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died by me in the land of Canaan in the way.” The shift seems abrupt, yet it follows naturally from what he has just done. Rachel bore him only two sons before she died giving birth to Benjamin (35:16-19). By adopting Joseph’s two sons, Jacob has in effect added two more sons to Rachel’s line. The woman he loved most, who once cried, “Give me children, or else I die” (30:1), is honoured after her death in the double portion given to her firstborn.

The memory also completes the reminiscence of verse 3. God appeared to Jacob at Luz on his return from Padan-aram, and Rachel died on the same journey, shortly afterward, on the road south. Both events happened “in the land of Canaan.” Rachel was buried there on the way to Ephrath, apart from the family cave at Machpelah. Her grave marked the first resting place of Jacob’s household in the promised land, and the pillar Jacob set over it was still known in the narrator’s day (35:20).

The words “died by me” can be rendered “died upon me” or “died to my sorrow.” The same small phrase appears in Jacob’s lament, “all these things are against me” (42:36). Even after many years, Jacob speaks of Rachel’s death as a blow that fell on him personally. Now, as he prepares for his own death, the grief returns, and he speaks of it to Rachel’s son.

The narrator adds, “the same is Beth-lehem.” The name points ahead. Jeremiah would picture Rachel weeping for her children as Israel went into exile (Jeremiah 31:15), and Matthew would hear that weeping again in Bethlehem when Herod killed the infants (Matthew 2:18). The village where Jacob buried his beloved wife would become the birthplace of the Son of David, the Redeemer to whom this whole family history leads.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “died upon me.” The preposition ‘al can express burden or loss falling on a person, so the phrase may mean “died to my grief” or “died, and it fell on me.” Jacob uses the same preposition when he says that the losses of Joseph, Simeon, and now Benjamin “are against me” (42:36). The expression conveys personal bereavement more than location.

verses.bibleText: And Israel beheld Joseph's sons, and said, Who are these?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel beheld Joseph’s sons, and said, Who are these?” Jacob has just spoken of the boys by name and claimed them as his own, so the question can hardly mean that he has never met them in seventeen years of living near Joseph. His eyesight is failing (v. 10), and he may make out only shapes standing beside his son. The question also serves the solemn character of the occasion. In an act of adoption and blessing the persons involved are formally identified, much as a minister at a wedding asks who gives the bride, though he knows the answer well.

Readers of Genesis cannot hear the question without remembering another bedside. Blind Isaac once asked, “Who art thou, my son?” and Jacob answered with a lie: “I am Esau thy firstborn” (27:18-19). Now Jacob is the old man asking, and the answer he receives will be true. The echo invites comparison all through the scene. The younger will again be preferred, yet nothing will be done in darkness or by deceit. The man who grasped a blessing by fraud has lived long enough to give one with open eyes of faith.

The question also reflects that the impulse to adopt did not come from the sight of two handsome young men. Jacob had declared his intention before he even recognized them, on the strength of God’s word at Luz.

wordNotes.explanation: The same two words Esau asked when he first saw Jacob’s wives and children approaching: “Who are those with thee?” (33:5). Jacob answered then that they were the children God had graciously given him, and Joseph now gives a strikingly similar reply (v. 9). The question echoes Isaac’s “Who art thou?” at the earlier blessing (27:18) but is answered honestly.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto his father, They are my sons, whom God hath given me in this place. And he said, Bring them, I pray thee, unto me, and I will bless them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph answers, “They are my sons, whom God hath given me in this place.” He credits God with his children, just as Jacob once told Esau that his family were “the children which God hath graciously given thy servant” (33:5). The son has learned the father’s faith. Throughout the Joseph story, Joseph speaks of God as the giver and director of events (41:16; 45:5-8), and he speaks of his sons in the same way.

“In this place” is Joseph’s way of naming Egypt without naming it. Jacob has been speaking of Luz, of Canaan, of the road to Ephrath; Joseph refers only to “this” place. The phrase is honest: these sons were born in Egypt, and their mother is Egyptian. Yet Joseph does not claim Egypt as their identity. They are gifts of God, received in a foreign land, and he brings them now to be joined to the family of promise.

Jacob replies, “Bring them, I pray thee, unto me, and I will bless them.” The old man does not command; he asks courteously, with the particle of entreaty, as one who longs for this moment. The verb “bless” carries the weight of the whole patriarchal story. From God’s first word to Abraham, “I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing” (12:2), blessing has passed down the chosen line. Jacob had once stolen it; now he is ready to give it freely.

wordNotes.term: וַאֲבָרְכֵם (va’avarekhem) — and I will bless them
wordNotes.explanation: From barakh, “to bless,” here with the first person and a plural object. In patriarchal narrative a father’s blessing was a solemn spoken act that conveyed God’s favour and announced the future of the one blessed; Isaac’s blessing, once spoken, could not be withdrawn (27:33). Jacob will speak as the channel of God’s blessing, calling on the God of his fathers to bless the lads (v. 16).

verses.bibleText: Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he could not see. And he brought them near unto him; and he kissed them, and embraced them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he could not see.” The narrator pauses to explain Jacob’s question in verse 8 and to prepare for what happens with his hands. The detail again sets this scene beside Isaac’s, where “his eyes were dim, so that he could not see” (27:1). In both cases a blind father must rely on touch and voice. What separates the two scenes is the spiritual sight of the one who blesses. Isaac, though blind, intended to bless Esau against God’s word; Jacob, though blind, will follow God’s purpose with full awareness.

Joseph “brought them near unto him; and he kissed them, and embraced them.” These two verbs together describe the warmest welcome in Genesis. Laban ran to meet Jacob, “embraced him, and kissed him” (29:13), and Esau ran to meet his brother and did the same (33:4). The old man, who had once believed he would go down to the grave mourning a son torn by beasts (37:33-35), now holds that son’s sons in his arms.

The gestures carry affection and also meaning. A father’s kiss and embrace publicly owned a child as his. The young men had just been declared Jacob’s sons in words; now he receives them with his body. The father in Jesus’ parable does the same when the lost son returns: he runs, falls on his neck, and kisses him before a word of the son’s confession is finished (Luke 15:20).

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “were heavy.” Kaved describes weight, and by extension dullness of the senses. Scripture speaks of ears made heavy so that they do not hear and of a hand too heavy to save. Isaac’s eyes in 27:1 were described with a different verb, meaning faint or dark, but the effect is the same. Jacob’s bodily sight is failing even as his spiritual discernment is about to be displayed.

verses.bibleText: And Israel said unto Joseph, I had not thought to see thy face: and, lo, God hath shewed me also thy seed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I had not thought to see thy face: and, lo, God hath shewed me also thy seed.” Jacob’s words compress the whole Joseph story into a sentence. For over twenty years he believed Joseph was dead. He had said, “I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning” (37:35). When the news came that Joseph lived, he could only say, “I will go and see him before I die” (45:28). Now he has seen not only Joseph’s face but Joseph’s children.

The verb changes subtly. Jacob had not expected “to see,” but God “hath shewed” him: the same verb in a causative form. What Jacob could not achieve or even hope for, God caused him to see. The grandfather looks back on his life and finds that God’s goodness has exceeded his expectations. Paul speaks of a God who is able to do “exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20), and Jacob is a living example.

The word “seed” is significant. Throughout Genesis it is the vocabulary of promise: the seed of the woman (3:15), the seed of Abraham (22:17-18), the seed to whom the land was promised (48:4). Jacob calls Joseph’s sons his “seed,” connecting these two young men with the covenant line. To see one’s children’s children was counted among the rewards of a life lived in God’s favour (Psalm 128:6).

The adoption began with Joseph naming God as the giver of his sons (v. 9). It ends with Jacob praising God for letting him see them. Both men speak of God first; the ceremony is framed in thanksgiving.

wordNotes.explanation: From palal, a verb that in this intensive form means to estimate, assess, or reckon, and is used of rendering judgment. In its reflexive form the same root is the ordinary Old Testament word for prayer, “to intercede.” Here, however, it simply means Jacob had not reckoned on such a thing; it would be a mistake to read prayer into the word. His expectations had been far smaller than God’s gift.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph brought them out from between his knees.” The young men had been drawn close to Jacob, at or beside his knees, as he kissed and embraced them. In the ancient world, placing a child on or by the knees was a recognized gesture of acceptance or adoption. Rachel had asked that Bilhah bear children “upon my knees” so that they would be counted as hers (30:3), and later Joseph himself will receive his great-grandchildren in the same way (50:23). With this gesture, the adoption is complete.

Then Joseph “bowed himself with his face to the earth.” The ruler of Egypt, before whom his own brothers had bowed in fulfilment of his dreams (42:6; 43:26), now prostrates himself before his father. He honours the patriarch who carries the promise of God. Whatever authority Joseph holds in Pharaoh’s court, in this room his father stands above him, as one through whom God speaks.

The bow is also the posture of a man preparing to receive a blessing. Joseph steps back with his sons, worships, and then arranges them for the next act. The scene shifts from adoption to benediction.

wordNotes.term: מֵעִם בִּרְכָּיו (me‘im birkav) — from between his knees
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “from with his knees.” The knees appear in several adoption or acceptance scenes: Bilhah bore children “upon” Rachel’s knees (30:3), and Machir’s children were “brought up upon Joseph’s knees” (50:23). Job asks why the knees received him at birth, the image of a parent receiving a newborn. Since the lads are about twenty, they were likely standing at Jacob’s knees, not sitting on them.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand, and brought them near unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph now arranges his sons with care. He takes “Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand.” Facing his father, Joseph positions the elder, Manasseh, directly before Jacob’s right hand and the younger, Ephraim, before his left. He brings them near, expecting the old man simply to stretch out his hands and bless them as they stand.

The right hand in Scripture is the hand of strength, honour, and favour. The LORD’s right hand is “glorious in power” and dashes the enemy in pieces (Exodus 15:6). The Messiah is invited to sit at God’s right hand (Psalm 110:1), and in the final judgment the sheep are set on the Judge’s right (Matthew 25:33). By placing Manasseh under his father’s right hand, Joseph intends the chief blessing to fall on the firstborn, as custom expected.

Joseph’s arrangement is natural and well-meant. He knows his father is nearly blind, and he wants to spare him any confusion. Yet the careful staging also reveals a settled assumption: that God’s blessing will follow the order of birth. That assumption is about to be overturned, and failing sight will have nothing to do with it.

wordNotes.explanation: The right hand represents power, skill, and the place of honour. Benjamin’s name, given by Jacob, means “son of the right hand” (35:18). Ecclesiastes contrasts the wise man’s heart “at his right hand” with the fool’s at his left. In blessing, the right hand conveyed the greater portion, which is why Joseph arranged his sons as he did.

verses.bibleText: And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim's head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh's head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh’s head.” To do this, Jacob must cross his arms, reaching his right hand across to the young man standing on his left, and his left across to the one on his right. The narrator adds two comments so that no reader can miss the point: Ephraim “was the younger,” and Jacob did it “wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.” This is no fumbling by a blind old man. Jacob knows which youth is which, and he deliberately sets the younger under the hand of greater blessing.

This is the first time Scripture records the laying on of hands as a sign of blessing. The gesture later became the recognized way of setting persons apart and conveying blessing or office. Moses laid his hands on Joshua to give him authority (Numbers 27:18-23); Jesus laid his hands on the children and blessed them (Mark 10:16); the apostles laid hands on the seven and on those who received the Spirit (Acts 6:6; 8:17). The hand itself has no magical power. It is an outward sign of an inward gift that God bestows.

The crossed hands gather up a pattern that runs through all of Genesis. Abel’s offering was accepted over Cain’s; Isaac was chosen over Ishmael; Jacob over Esau; Joseph over his elder brothers; Perez broke out ahead of Zerah (38:29). Again and again God bypasses the expectations attached to birth order to show that his blessing is a gift. Paul draws exactly this lesson from Jacob and Esau: before the twins were born or had done good or evil, God declared that “the elder shall serve the younger,” so that his purpose might stand “not of works, but of him that calleth” (Romans 9:11-12). Ephraim’s blessing is an act of grace.

There is also a moving reversal in Jacob’s own story. As a young man he deceived his blind father to seize the blessing meant for the firstborn. Now, blind himself, he gives the greater blessing to the younger openly and honestly, in obedience to God. Hebrews singles out this moment as the sum of Jacob’s faith: “By faith Jacob, when he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph” (Hebrews 11:21). The grasping supplanter has become a man who blesses according to God’s will.

wordNotes.term: שִׂכֵּל אֶת־יָדָיו (sikkel ’et-yadav) — guiding his hands wittingly
wordNotes.explanation: The verb sakal usually means to act prudently or with insight, and in its causative form to instruct or give understanding. Here it describes Jacob directing his hands with full intent. Some take it from a similar root meaning “to cross,” and the Greek Old Testament renders the phrase “crossing his hands.” Either way, the narrator stresses that the action was purposeful. The same verb describes David behaving wisely and God promising to “instruct” those who trust him.

verses.bibleText: And he blessed Joseph, and said, God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac did walk, the God which fed me all my life long unto this day,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he blessed Joseph.” Jacob’s hands rest on the heads of the two lads, yet the narrator says he blessed Joseph. The father is blessed in his sons; the double portion given to Ephraim and Manasseh is Joseph’s portion. Whatever distinction Jacob makes between the brothers, the blessing as a whole honours Rachel’s firstborn.

The blessing begins with three descriptions of God, each one longer and more personal than the last, running through verse 16. The first is “God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac did walk.” To walk before God is to live openly in his presence, answerable to him and sustained by him. God told Abraham, “walk before me, and be thou perfect” (17:1), and Abraham later described himself as one who walked before the LORD (24:40). Jacob places his grandsons in a line of faith that stretches back two generations. The God who will bless them is the God whom their forefathers trusted and obeyed.

The second description is “the God which fed me all my life long unto this day.” The verb is the shepherd’s word: God has shepherded Jacob, leading, feeding, and protecting him. Jacob knew the work of a shepherd from the inside. He had spent twenty years tending Laban’s flocks in heat and frost, losing sleep, answering for every lost animal (31:38-40). Looking back over a life full of flight, exile, grief, and fear, he sees that he had a Shepherd the whole time. This is the first time Scripture calls God a shepherd, and Jacob will use the image again in his blessing of Joseph, speaking of “the shepherd, the stone of Israel” (49:24).

The image runs through the rest of the Bible. David would sing, “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). Isaiah promised that God would feed his flock and gather the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11). Jesus took the title for himself: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The aged patriarch, in his last days, names the same Shepherd who would one day lay down his life for the flock.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the one shepherding me.” Ra‘ah means to pasture or tend a flock, including feeding, guiding, and guarding it. Abel was a “keeper [ro‘eh] of sheep” (4:2), and Joseph’s brothers told Pharaoh, “Thy servants are shepherds” (47:3). Jacob applies the familiar occupation of his family to God himself. The KJV “fed” captures one part of the shepherd’s work, but the word includes the whole of his care.

wordNotes.term: הִתְהַלְּכוּ לְפָנָיו (hithallekhu lefanav) — did walk before him
wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form of halakh, “to walk,” implying a continuing way of life. Enoch and Noah “walked with God” (5:22; 6:9); Abraham was commanded to walk “before” God (17:1). Walking before someone suggests living in view of a master who sees and approves. The phrase describes faithful conduct in fellowship with God, the life that faith produces.

verses.bibleText: The Angel which redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads; and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third and climactic description is “The Angel which redeemed me from all evil.” In the Hebrew poetry of the blessing, this line stands in parallel with the two before it: the God before whom his fathers walked, the God who shepherded him, the Angel who redeemed him. All three are the subject of a single verb, “bless,” which is singular. Jacob calls on one God, described in three ways. No created angel could stand in a sentence like this, sharing God’s place as the source of blessing.

Jacob had met this Angel at critical moments. The “angel of God” spoke to him in a dream at Haran and said, “I am the God of Bethel” (31:11-13). At the Jabbok a “man” wrestled with him until daybreak, blessed him, and renamed him; Jacob called the place Peniel, “for I have seen God face to face” (32:24-30). Hosea, recalling that night, says Jacob “had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him,” and then calls the same one “the LORD God of hosts” (Hosea 12:4-5). The Angel of the LORD in Genesis speaks as God, receives worship, and is yet distinguished from the Father who sends him (16:10-13; 22:11-18). This is the Son of God before his incarnation, the one Isaiah calls “the angel of his presence” who saved and redeemed Israel (Isaiah 63:9), and whom Paul identifies as the Rock that followed Israel: “that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

The verb “redeemed” appears here for the first time in Scripture. A redeemer, go’el, was the near kinsman who stepped in to buy back a relative’s land or freedom (Leviticus 25:25, 48; Ruth 4:4-6). Jacob looks back on a life threatened by Esau’s anger, Laban’s schemes, famine, and the apparent loss of Joseph, and confesses that a divine Kinsman delivered him “from all evil.” The New Testament reveals the full price of this redemption: Christ “gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity” (Titus 2:14).

Then comes the petition: “bless the lads; and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac.” To have the patriarchs’ names named on them means that Ephraim and Manasseh will be counted as Israel, heirs of the covenant made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The boy called Manasseh, “making to forget,” will never be allowed to forget his father’s house; his name will carry Israel’s.

Finally, Jacob prays, “let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth.” The prayer was answered: Moses would speak of “the ten thousands of Ephraim” and “the thousands of Manasseh” (Deuteronomy 33:17).

wordNotes.term: הַמַּלְאָךְ הַגֹּאֵל (hammal’akh hago’el) — the Angel which redeemed
wordNotes.explanation: Mal’akh means messenger, human or heavenly; the article points to a particular Messenger Jacob had known. Go’el is the participle of ga’al, the kinsman-redeemer who rescues a relative from debt, slavery, or wrong. This is its first use in Scripture. Later the same word describes God redeeming Israel from Egypt “with a stretched out arm” and calls the LORD Israel’s Redeemer. The parallel with “God” in verse 15 and the singular verb “bless” identify this Angel as God himself, revealed in the person of the Son.

wordNotes.term: וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב (veyidgu larov) — and let them grow into a multitude
wordNotes.explanation: The verb dagah occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Many connect it with dag, “fish,” picturing increase like the swarming creatures of the sea that God blessed at creation (1:22). The link is possible but uncertain, and the sense is clear from the following word, “abundance.” Jacob asks that Joseph’s sons multiply greatly in the land.

verses.bibleText: And when Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand upon the head of Ephraim, it displeased him: and he held up his father's hand, to remove it from Ephraim's head unto Manasseh's head.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph sees where his father’s right hand rests, “and it displeased him.” The Hebrew says literally that it was evil in his eyes. He assumes that his father’s failing sight has caused a mistake, and he takes hold of Jacob’s hand to lift it from Ephraim’s head and move it to Manasseh’s. The ruler of Egypt, used to setting things in order, tries to correct the patriarch.

Joseph’s reaction is understandable and has a long precedent. When God promised Abraham a son by Sarah, Abraham pleaded for Ishmael, his firstborn (17:18), and the matter was “very grievous” in his sight when Ishmael had to be sent away (21:11). Parents naturally expect the eldest to inherit first place. Joseph himself, the favoured younger son, ought to have remembered that God does not always follow that rule; yet when it came to his own children, he assumed the custom would hold. His hand on his father’s hand is a picture of the human impulse to steer God’s blessing along the lines we expect.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינָיו (vayyera‘ be‘enav) — it displeased him
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “it was evil in his eyes.” The idiom expresses strong disapproval, not moral evil in the act itself. It describes Abraham’s distress at sending Ishmael away (21:11) and Samuel’s displeasure when Israel demanded a king. The phrase reveals Joseph’s judgment of the situation, which the following verses show to be mistaken.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto his father, Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn; put thy right hand upon his head.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn; put thy right hand upon his head.” Joseph speaks respectfully, calling Jacob “my father,” but firmly. His argument rests on a single fact: Manasseh is the firstborn. In Joseph’s mind that settles the question.

The words “this is the firstborn” must have struck Jacob with peculiar force. Decades earlier he had stood before Isaac and claimed, falsely, “I am Esau thy firstborn” (27:19). His whole early life had been a struggle over the rights of the firstborn, a struggle he pursued by bargaining and deceit. Now his son urges the claim of birth upon him. Jacob has learned through long discipline that the blessing belongs to God to give, and that God had decided between the twins before they were born (25:23). The firstborn’s privileges were real, protected later in law (Deuteronomy 21:17), but they were never meant to bind God’s freedom to choose.

wordNotes.explanation: Bekhor denotes the first son, who normally received a double share of the inheritance and leadership of the family. Yet in Scripture the term also describes rank conferred by God apart from birth. God calls Israel “my firstborn” among the nations, declares “Ephraim is my firstborn,” and promises of David’s heir, “I will make him my firstborn.” Ephraim was not born first, yet he is named firstborn by God’s choice.

verses.bibleText: And his father refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And his father refused.” The verb is strong: Jacob will not be moved. The weak old man, who needed help to sit up, holds his hands in place against the grip of Egypt’s second ruler. Yet his answer is gentle: “I know it, my son, I know it.” The repetition reassures Joseph that his father is neither confused nor careless. He knows which head lies under which hand, and he knows that Manasseh was born first. He acts with full understanding.

The contrast with Isaac is complete. Isaac blessed Jacob without knowing whom he blessed, and afterward “trembled very exceedingly” at what he had done (27:33). Jacob blesses knowingly, according to a purpose he has come to see. If Isaac’s unwitting blessing stood, how much more firmly this deliberate one.

Manasseh is not set aside. “He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great.” The repeated “he also” assures Joseph that his firstborn will share richly in the blessing. Unlike Ishmael or Esau, Manasseh remains within the covenant people and becomes one of Israel’s largest tribes, with lands on both sides of the Jordan. The difference between the brothers is one of degree: “his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.”

The prophecy proved true over time. At the first census in the wilderness Ephraim outnumbered Manasseh; at the second Manasseh was larger (Numbers 1:33-35; 26:34, 37). But from the days of Joshua, an Ephraimite, the tribe rose to leadership among the northern tribes, and when the kingdom divided, the northern nation was often called simply “Ephraim” (Isaiah 7:2; Hosea 4:17). Jacob’s words proved to be more than a fond grandfather’s wish. They were a prophetic blessing, given by the Spirit of God and fulfilled in history.

The phrase “multitude of nations” is literally “fullness of the nations.” Paul uses a closely related expression for the full number of Gentiles brought into God’s people (Romans 11:25). Whether or not Paul had this verse in mind, the pattern is the same: God’s blessing reaches beyond the expected heirs to gather a great company by grace.

wordNotes.term: יָדַעְתִּי בְנִי יָדַעְתִּי (yada‘ti veni yada‘ti) — I know it, my son, I know it
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled verb frames the tender address “my son,” combining firmness with affection. Yada‘ means to know by experience and understanding. Jacob’s knowledge contrasts with Isaac’s ignorance in chapter 27 and with Joseph’s assumption in verse 18. In Scripture, God’s knowledge often grounds his choices, as when he says of Abraham, “I know him” (18:19).

Literally “the fullness of the nations.” Melo’ means that which fills something completely, as in “the earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof.” The promise to Jacob that “a company of nations” would come from him (35:11) is here focused on Ephraim. The Greek translation of Genesis renders it “multitude of nations,” but Paul’s “fulness [plērōma] of the Gentiles” in Romans 11:25 reflects the same Hebrew idea of completeness.

verses.bibleText: And he blessed them that day, saying, In thee shall Israel bless, saying, God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh: and he set Ephraim before Manasseh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he blessed them that day.” The narrator sums up the blessing and adds its final words, now addressed directly to the young men: “In thee shall Israel bless, saying, God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh.” The “thee” is singular, spoken to each of them in turn. Their names will become a formula of blessing in Israel. When later Israelites wished God’s favour on a son, they would hold up Ephraim and Manasseh as the picture of what blessing looks like.

The saying echoes God’s first promise to Abraham: “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed” (12:3). Within Israel, the Joseph tribes become a living example of that promise, a standard for fruitfulness and divine favour. The elders at Bethlehem would bless Ruth in a similar way, praying that she would be like Rachel and Leah, “which two did build the house of Israel” (Ruth 4:11). Jewish families have long kept the custom of blessing their sons with these very words on the eve of the Sabbath, carrying Jacob’s benediction across the generations.

The verse closes with the narrator’s own summary: “and he set Ephraim before Manasseh.” Even in the wording of the blessing formula, Ephraim’s name comes first. Jacob’s decision is final and public. What began with crossed hands is sealed in words that the whole nation will repeat.

It is worth noticing what the formula does not say. It does not wish for Ephraim and Manasseh to be like their Egyptian grandfather, the priest of On, or like the court of Pharaoh where they grew up. The model of blessing is two sons of Egypt who were brought into Israel by adoption. Those who once stood outside the covenant family become the pattern of God’s favour within it, a foretaste of the gospel by which those who were “far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

wordNotes.term: בְּךָ יְבָרֵךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל (bekha yevarekh yisra’el) — in thee shall Israel bless
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “by you Israel will bless.” To bless “by” someone means to use that person’s name as the model in a spoken blessing. The opposite use appears in Jeremiah, where the fate of two false prophets becomes a curse formula: “The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab.” Here Ephraim and Manasseh become the positive standard. “Israel” refers to the people as a whole, the nation that will grow from Jacob’s sons.

verses.bibleText: And Israel said unto Joseph, Behold, I die: but God shall be with you, and bring you again unto the land of your fathers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob turns from the grandsons to their father. “Behold, I die: but God shall be with you, and bring you again unto the land of your fathers.” The words are plain and unflinching. Jacob does not soften the fact of his death or speak of it as passing into another life. He is about to “sleep with my fathers,” as he put it when asking to be buried in Canaan (47:30). Death is the end of his part in the story, and he says so.

Yet the sentence turns on the word “but.” Jacob’s death does not end God’s faithfulness. “God shall be with you.” The pronoun is plural; Jacob now looks beyond Joseph to the whole family that will remain in Egypt. The promise God gave Jacob at Bethel, “I am with thee, and will keep thee... and will bring thee again into this land” (28:15), and repeated as he set out for Egypt, “I will also surely bring thee up again” (46:4), Jacob now hands on to his descendants. The patriarch passes; the God of the patriarch remains.

“The land of your fathers” identifies Canaan as the family’s true home, though Joseph has lived in Egypt since boyhood and his sons have never seen anywhere else. Jacob will be carried there for burial within weeks (50:13), but the larger return lies centuries ahead, at the exodus. Joseph understood. On his own deathbed he would speak almost the same words to his brothers, “I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land,” and make them swear to carry his bones up from Egypt (50:24-25). Moses kept that oath (Exodus 13:19).

Hebrews says of the patriarchs that “these all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Hebrews 11:13), and that God has provided something better, so that they will not be made perfect apart from those who come after them (Hebrews 11:39-40). Their hope did not lie in some conscious existence immediately after death. It looked forward to the day when God would raise them to receive the inheritance in person. Jacob’s “I die: but God” is the confession of every believer who faces death trusting the One who is with his people and who will bring them home.

wordNotes.term: הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מֵת (hinneh ’anokhi met) — behold, I die
wordNotes.explanation: The participle met describes death as imminent, “I am about to die.” Joseph repeats it at the end of Genesis, and Moses uses it before Israel crosses the Jordan. When a leader announces his death in these passages, it is followed by a word about God’s continuing care for those left behind. Hinneh draws attention to the solemn announcement.

wordNotes.term: וְהָיָה אֱלֹהִים עִמָּכֶם (vehayah ’elohim ‘immakhem) — God shall be with you
wordNotes.explanation: The promise of God’s presence, “with you,” runs through the patriarchal stories (26:3; 28:15; 39:2). Here it is plural, extended from Joseph to the whole family. The same assurance was given to Moses and Joshua and echoes in the name Immanuel, “God with us.” Jesus closed his earthly ministry with it: “I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.”

verses.bibleText: Moreover I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Moreover I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren.” Jacob ends with a personal gift to Joseph. The word translated “portion” is shekem, which ordinarily means “shoulder” and is also the name of the town of Shechem. The meaning “portion” is not found elsewhere and depends largely on the ancient versions. Jacob very likely intends a play on words: he gives Joseph a “shoulder” or ridge of land, the plot near Shechem that he had bought from the sons of Hamor (33:18-19). Joseph’s bones were later buried in that very field (Joshua 24:32), and in Jesus’ day the ground near Sychar was still remembered as “the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph” (John 4:5). Jesus met the Samaritan woman beside the well there.

The second half of the verse is harder: the land “which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.” Elsewhere Jacob acquired the Shechem plot by purchase, and he condemned the violence of Simeon and Levi against the town (34:30; 49:5-7). No other passage records Jacob himself fighting. One reasonable explanation is that after Jacob moved south, the local inhabitants, here called by the general name “Amorite,” seized his property, and he later had to recover it by force. Scripture does not supply the details, and it is wise not to press beyond what the text says. What is clear is that Jacob regards the land as his to give and gives it to Joseph above his brothers.

The gift is another act of faith. Neither Jacob nor Joseph would ever live on that ground again; Joseph would only be buried there, after the exodus and the conquest. Jacob bestows land his family cannot enjoy for centuries, trusting God to bring them back as he has just promised. Later, when Israel did take the land, God would remind them that it was given “not with thy sword, nor with thy bow” (Joshua 24:12). Every inheritance in the land of promise was finally God’s gift.

wordNotes.explanation: Shekhem means “shoulder,” the place where burdens are carried (9:23; 21:14), and by extension perhaps a ridge or slope of land. It is also the name of the city of Shechem, where Jacob bought land and where Joseph was later buried. The rendering “portion” rests mainly on the ancient versions. The wordplay links Jacob’s gift to the place that would hold Joseph’s bones.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would you most want to pass on to the next generation if you knew you had only one conversation left?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Dying Jacob hands on God’s promise by faith: he adopts Joseph’s Egyptian-born sons into Israel, sets the younger first as God directs, and trusts the Shepherd and Redeemer of his own life to keep his descendants and bring them home.
discussionQuestions: Why does Jacob begin with what God said to him at Luz before he says anything about Joseph’s sons?
What did Ephraim and Manasseh gain by being counted as Jacob’s sons instead of Egyptian nobility?
How does this blessing scene differ from Isaac’s blessing in Genesis 27, and what has changed in Jacob?
What do Jacob’s three names for God in verses 15-16 reveal about how he understood his own life?
Why does Hebrews 11:21 choose this moment, of all Jacob’s life, as the example of his faith?
commonMisunderstandings: Jacob did not cross his hands because he was confused or blind; the text says he did it knowingly and refused to change it.
Preferring the younger does not mean Manasseh was cursed or left out; both received blessing, and Ephraim was first among brothers.
The redeeming Angel is no created angel receiving prayer; Jacob sets him in parallel with God as the source of blessing, the divine Messenger who met him at Bethel and Peniel.
Jacob’s words “I die” do not express despair or a belief that he was passing into another life; his hope rests on God’s presence with his family and his promise of the land.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God at the centre of the scene. Jacob’s authority to adopt and bless comes from God’s word at Luz; the crossed hands follow God’s choice and overturn the custom of birth; the blessing calls on the God who shepherded and redeemed Jacob; and the final promise rests on God being with the family after the patriarch is gone.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The God who took two Egyptian-born young men and gave them a name in Israel offers you a place in his family by grace; receive his blessing, trust the Redeemer who has carried you this far, and live toward the home he has promised.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Salvation by grace through faith: God adopts into his family those who have no claim by birth, blesses by his own choice, and redeems through the divine Angel who is the pre-incarnate Christ, while his people face death with hope in his promise.
flow: Ephraim and Manasseh were born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother, outsiders to the promise until Jacob claimed them as his own.
Jacob crossed his hands and set the younger first, showing that God’s blessing follows his gracious choice and not human rank.
Jacob credited his whole life to the Shepherd God and the Angel who redeemed him from all evil, the Son of God who would come in flesh to redeem us.
Facing death, Jacob rested his hope on God’s presence and promise rather than on his own survival.
Christ invites us to be adopted as God’s children, to receive his blessing by faith, and to wait for the inheritance he will give at his return.
simpleIllustrations: A family court adoption gives a child a new surname and full rights of inheritance in a single act; Jacob’s words “they are mine” did the same for Joseph’s sons.
A grandfather who deliberately crosses his arms to reach the smaller child shows that his choice was intentional; God’s grace works with the same deliberate love.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you accept the place God offers you in his family, not by birth or merit but by his grace, and trust the Redeemer who has watched over your life?
cautions: Do not turn the preference for Ephraim into a doctrine that God arbitrarily rejects some people; the chapter blesses both brothers.
Avoid presenting the redeeming Angel as a created angel to whom believers should pray; Scripture identifies the Angel with God himself.
Do not use the chapter to suggest that the dead enter conscious bliss at once; Jacob’s hope looks to God’s future acts for his family.

reflectionQuestions: Can I name the ways God has shepherded me “all my life long unto this day”?
Do I see my place in God’s family as a gift of grace rather than something owed to me?
When God’s choices cross my expectations, as Jacob’s hands crossed Joseph’s plan, how do I respond?
What am I handing on to the next generation: possessions only, or the promises of God?
Does the thought of my own death rest on the assurance that God will be with those I leave behind?
